> 
> # 19705. Opportunity Blackboard
> 
> Shared objects:
> 
> ```text
> Signals
> Hypotheses
> Counterarguments
> Evidence
> Unknowns
> Experiments
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19706. This avoids conversational duplication.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19707. Opportunity Hypothesis Template
> 
> ```yaml
> hypothesis:
>   problem:
>     ...
>   proposed_mechanism:
>     ...
>   enabling_capabilities:
>     ...
>   expected_benefit:
>     ...
>   critical_unknowns:
>     ...
>   evidence:
>     ...
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19708. `expected_benefit`
> 
> should be:
> 
> ```text
> Claim/Hypothesis
> ```
> 
> unless measured.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19709. Example:
> 
> ```text
> may reduce integration time
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19710. Do not write:
> 
> ```text
> will reduce integration time by 70%
> ```
> 
> without evidence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19711. Opportunity Assumptions
> 
> Explicit list.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19712. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Assumption A:
> users will share spare lab capacity.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19713. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Assumption B:
> equipment calendars can be exposed securely.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19714. Each assumption can become:
> 
> ```text
> validation task
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19715. This turns innovation into testable process.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19716. Assumption Graph
> 
> Some assumptions depend on others.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19717. Example:
> 
> ```text
> shared lab market viable
> ```
> 
> requires:
> 
> ```text
> capacity exists
> +
> demand exists
> +
> booking interoperability
> +
> legal access possible
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19718. If first condition false:
> 
> stop.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19719. This saves investigation cost.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19720. Hypothesis Decomposition
> 
> Innovation Hypothesis:
> 
> ```text
> Shared Federated Lab Network
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19721. Sub-hypotheses:
> 
> ```text
> sufficient idle capacity
> external demand exists
> semantic equipment profiles can normalize supply
> cross-org booking legally/operationally possible
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19722. Each can be tested independently.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19723. Evidence Ladder
> 
> Opportunity evidence may progress:
> 
> ```text
> ANECTODAL
> OBSERVATIONAL
> REPEATED_OBSERVATION
> PILOT
> CONTROLLED_TEST
> OPERATIONAL
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19724. Do not force all domains into same exact ladder.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19725. But concept useful:
> 
> ```text
> evidence maturity
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19726. Opportunity Readiness
> 
> Dimensions:
> 
> ```text
> problem evidence
> technical evidence
> resource evidence
> economic evidence
> organizational evidence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19727. Example:
> 
> ```text
> technical evidence = strong
> market demand = unknown
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19728. Another:
> 
> ```text
> demand = strong
> technology = research-only
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19729. Very different next steps.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19730. Next-Best-Evidence Action
> 
> Engine asks:
> 
> ```text
> What cheapest useful action
> would reduce the most important uncertainty?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19731. Example:
> 
> Before building platform,
> 
> ask 10 laboratories:
> 
> ```text
> would you expose spare slots?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19732. Or inspect historical utilization data.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19733. Example technology transfer:
> 
> Before manufacturing robot skin,
> 
> test:
> 
> ```text
> does fiber signal distinguish contact from bending?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19734. This may be a tiny experiment.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19735. Opportunity Engine integrates Value of Information.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19736. Evidence action types
> 
> ```text
> SEARCH
> INTERVIEW
> BENCHMARK
> SIMULATION
> PROTOTYPE
> EXPERIMENT
> PILOT
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19737. `SEARCH`
> 
> cheap.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19738. `INTERVIEW`
> 
> useful for demand/organizational assumptions.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19739. `BENCHMARK`
> 
> technical.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19740. `SIMULATION`
> 
> useful but not reality.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19741. `PROTOTYPE`
> 
> tests integration.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19742. `EXPERIMENT`
> 
> tests specific causal/technical claim.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19743. `PILOT`
> 
> tests in realistic operational context.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19744. Progressive Commitment
> 
> Do not jump:
> 
> ```text
> idea → full project
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19745. Better:
> 
> ```text
> Hypothesis
> ↓
> Desk Research
> ↓
> Small Experiment
> ↓
> Pilot
> ↓
> Program
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19746. This integrates Adaptive Strategy.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19747. Kill Criteria
> 
> Every hypothesis should ideally define:
> 
> ```text
> what evidence would cause us to stop?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19748. Example:
> 
> ```text
> If sensor latency > 100 ms
> under realistic conditions,
> discard real-time grasp-control path.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19749. Kill Criteria prevent sunk-cost escalation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19750. Pivot Criteria
> 
> Maybe original target fails,
> 
> but another application emerges.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19751. Example fiber sensor too slow for grasp control,
> 
> but useful for:
> 
> ```text
> structural robot skin health monitoring
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19752. Then:
> 
> ```text
> new Opportunity Hypothesis
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19753. Do not silently redefine success.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19754. Original hypothesis can be:
> 
> ```text
> REFUTED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19755. New hypothesis:
> 
> ```text
> FORMULATED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19756. This preserves scientific integrity.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19757. Opportunity Portfolio
> 
> System may have thousands of hypotheses.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19758. Need portfolio view.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19759. Dimensions:
> 
> ```text
> domain
> problem type
> evidence maturity
> resource needs
> time horizon
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19760. Avoid one ranked list.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19761. Better clusters:
> 
> ```text
> quick tests
> long-term research
> infrastructure
> cross-domain
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19762. Strategic Program can select subset.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19763. Opportunity Aging
> 
> Old hypothesis may become stale.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19764. Example:
> 
> ```text
> technology gap from 2024
> ```
> 
> may disappear in 2026.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19765. Recheck:
> 
> ```text
> problem still exists?
> technology changed?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19766. Status:
> 
> ```text
> STALE_REVIEW_REQUIRED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19767. Archived hypotheses can be reactivated.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19768. Opportunity Revival
> 
> Trigger:
> 
> ```text
> new technology
> new cost
> new regulation
> new evidence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19769. Example idea previously infeasible due to:
> 
> ```text
> GPU cost
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19770. New hardware changes economics.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19771. System reopens.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19772. This is useful for long-term research memory.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19773. Opportunity Provenance
> 
> Every hypothesis should answer:
> 
> ```text
> Where did this idea come from?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19774. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Gap cluster G12
> Paper P77
> Repo R9
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19775. This prevents:
> 
> ```text
> AI idea with no traceable basis
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19776. Pure generative hypothesis can exist.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19777. But label:
> 
> ```text
> GENERATIVE
> ```
> 
> and evidence initially absent.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19778. That is acceptable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19779. It just receives lower evidentiary status,
> 
> not automatic rejection.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19780. Opportunity Prior Art Search
> 
> Before calling idea novel:
> 
> ```text
> search existing products
> papers
> repos
> standards
> projects
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19781. Possible outcomes:
> 
> ```text
> KNOWN_SOLUTION
> PARTIAL_SOLUTION
> RELATED_PRIOR_ART
> NO_MATCH_FOUND
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19782. `NO_MATCH_FOUND` ≠ novel.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19783. It means:
> 
> ```text
> search did not find prior art
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19784. Important epistemic precision.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19785. Existing solution may actually strengthen opportunity.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19786. Example:
> 
> ```text
> similar product exists in aerospace
> ```
> 
> but not robotics.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19787. This gives transfer evidence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19788. Opportunity vs Invention
> 
> An Opportunity can be:
> 
> ```text
> adopt existing
> combine existing
> standardize existing
> invent new
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19789. Innovation Engine should not bias toward invention.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19790. Often best opportunity is:
> 
> ```text
> reuse
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19791. Example repeated software gaps solved by existing OSS library.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19792. Then opportunity:
> 
> ```text
> institutional adoption/package
> ```
> 
> not new algorithm.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19793. Technology Transfer Maturity
> 
> Possible progression:
> 
> ```text
> ANALOGY
> MECHANISM_PLAUSIBLE
> LAB_TESTED
> DOMAIN_PILOTED
> OPERATIONAL
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19794. Again status descriptive.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19795. Example fiber sensing:
> 
> ```text
> ANALOGY
> ```
> 
> first.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19796. Small experiment shows contact detectable:
> 
> ```text
> MECHANISM_PLAUSIBLE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19797. Robot finger test:
> 
> ```text
> LAB_TESTED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19798. Full gripper:
> 
> ```text
> DOMAIN_PILOTED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19799. Production robot:
> 
> ```text
> OPERATIONAL
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19800. Technology Transfer Package
> 
> Once transfer validated,
> 
> create reusable:
> 
> ```text
> Transfer Pattern
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19801. Contains:
> 
> ```text
> source principle
> target function
> required adaptations
> known limitations
> evidence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19802. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Fiber strain sensing
> → robotic surface sensing
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19803. Future projects can reuse.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19804. Cross-Domain Knowledge Graph
> 
> Domains themselves can be Concepts.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19805. Example:
> 
> ```text
> robotics
> photonics
> civil engineering
> biomedicine
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19806. Technology transfer edges connect:
> 
> ```text
> principles
> functions
> implementations
> ```
> 
> across them.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19807. This can create:
> 
> # Technology Transfer Map
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19808. 2D visualization:
> 
> ```text
> Domain A
> ↔ shared capability
> ↔ Domain B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19809. High-density bridges may reveal:
> 
> ```text
> innovation corridors
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19810. Example:
> 
> ```text
> photonics ↔ robotics
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19811. Another:
> 
> ```text
> game engines ↔ scientific digital twins
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19812. Another:
> 
> ```text
> MMORPG interest management ↔ industrial spatial twins
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19813. This last example is directly relevant.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19814. MMORPG technology provides:
> 
> ```text
> large world state
> interest management
> entity synchronization
> distributed clients
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19815. Industrial twin needs:
> 
> ```text
> many moving objects
> partial views
> state synchronization
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19816. Shared functional structures produce transfer hypothesis.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19817. But differences:
> 
> ```text
> real-world safety
> uncertainty
> privacy
> authority
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19818. These must be added.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19819. Technology Transfer can therefore be:
> 
> ```text
> reuse with adaptation
> ```
> 
> not direct transplant.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19820. Adaptation Gap
> 
> Explicit object/view:
> 
> ```text
> what must change
> for source technology
> to work in target domain?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19821. Example game engine → port digital twin
> 
> Adaptation gaps:
> 
> ```text
> real telemetry integration
> bitemporal state
> safety semantics
> uncertainty
> real identity
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19822. This creates implementation roadmap.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19823. Cross-Industry Search
> 
> Opportunity Engine can ask:
> 
> ```text
> Who already solved structurally similar problem?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19824. Example target:
> 
> ```text
> tracking thousands of moving containers
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19825. Analogous domains:
> 
> ```text
> MMORPG entities
> warehouse robots
> air traffic
> fleet logistics
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19826. Each may provide transferable techniques.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19827. This resembles:
> 
> ```text
> solution-by-analogy
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19828. Domain Distance
> 
> Far domains may produce more novel ideas,
> 
> but also higher adaptation risk.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19829. Do not automatically reward distance.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19830. Show:
> 
> ```text
> semantic similarity
> domain distance
> adaptation gaps
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19831. Opportunity Engine can deliberately search:
> 
> ```text
> near analogies
> ```
> 
> and:
> 
> ```text
> far analogies
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19832. Near analogy:
> 
> ```text
> industrial robot
> ↔ warehouse robot
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19833. Far analogy:
> 
> ```text
> MMORPG world streaming
> ↔ port digital twin
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19834. Far analogies are useful exploratory source,
> 
> not stronger evidence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19835. Concept Combination Search
> 
> Another innovation mechanism:
> 
> ```text
> Capability A
> +
> Capability B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19836. Search whether combination already used.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19837. Example:
> 
> ```text
> semantic M2M
> +
> procedural graphs
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19838. Potential:
> 
> ```text
> distributed typed agent workflow network
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19839. But combinatorial explosion enormous.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19840. Need relevance filters.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19841. Combination candidates should share:
> 
> ```text
> compatible interfaces
> complementary functions

> # 19958. Innovation Hypothesis Compiler
> 
> Input:
> 
> ```text
> signals
> patterns
> analogies
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19959. Output normalized:
> 
> ```text
> Problem
> Mechanism
> Capabilities
> Expected Outcome
> Unknowns
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19960. This prevents vague ideas.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19961. Example vague:
> 
> ```text
> Use AI for logistics.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19962. Compiler should reject as too underspecified.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19963. Better:
> 
> ```text
> Use predictive berth-state estimation
> to reduce uncertainty
> in berth assignment.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19964. Then:
> 
> ```text
> measurable variables
> ```
> 
> exist.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19965. Hypothesis Quality Gate
> 
> Minimum:
> 
> ```text
> target problem
> mechanism
> context
> testable implication
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19966. If missing:
> 
> ```text
> DRAFT
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19967. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Blockchain for laboratories
> ```
> 
> without mechanism:
> 
> low-quality hypothesis.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19968. The system asks:
> 
> ```text
> What problem?
> What function?
> Why blockchain?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19969. This protects against buzzword-driven innovation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19970. Technology-Neutral Problem Formulation
> 
> Before proposing technology,
> 
> represent problem without solution.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19971. Example bad:
> 
> ```text
> Need an AI chatbot for equipment booking.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19972. Better problem:
> 
> ```text
> Users cannot efficiently discover
> and reserve suitable equipment.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19973. Solutions may be:
> 
> ```text
> search UI
> semantic registry
> agent
> marketplace
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19974. AI chatbot is only one implementation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19975. Opportunity Engine should separate:
> 
> ```text
> Problem
> ```
> 
> from:
> 
> ```text
> Proposed Solution
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19976. Same for technology scouting.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19977. Problem Root Cause
> 
> Repeated symptom may have deeper cause.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19978. Example:
> 
> ```text
> projects repeatedly miss deadlines
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19979. Possible causes:
> 
> ```text
> resource scarcity
> bad planning
> approval latency
> dependency uncertainty
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19980. Opportunity should address:
> 
> ```text
> causal mechanism
> ```
> 
> not just symptom.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19981. Causal Engine integration
> 
> Opportunity hypothesis can state:
> 
> ```text
> Intervention X
> may change Outcome Y
> through mechanism M.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19982. Example:
> 
> ```text

> → higher equipment utilization
> → shorter project delays
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 19983. These are causal Claims,
> 
> not guaranteed.

> 
> # 19984. Experiment/pilot can test.

> ---
>

> 
> ```text

Продолжаю с **20139**. Теперь соединяем Opportunity, System Synthesis и Runtime в уровень **Mission Control**: одна большая цель автоматически раскладывается на согласованный Program, портфель взаимозависимых Projects, общие ресурсы, milestones, decision gates и адаптивное перепланирование.

> является Artifact/Capability outcome.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20173. Example
> 
> ```text
> trained operators
> ```
> 
> является Human Capability outcome.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20174. Program Synthesis должен различать эти типы.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20175. Центральная задача
> 
> ```text
> Mission Outcome
> ↓
> Which Programs are required?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20176. Program Archetypes
> 
> Полезный library:
> 
> ```text
> RESEARCH_PROGRAM
> ENGINEERING_PROGRAM
> INFRASTRUCTURE_PROGRAM
> STANDARDIZATION_PROGRAM
> DEPLOYMENT_PROGRAM
> CAPABILITY_BUILDING_PROGRAM
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20177. Это archetypes,
> 
> не новые roots.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20178. Example tactile Mission может получить:
> 
> ```text
> Research Program
> Engineering Integration Program
> Validation Program
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20179. Funding может быть:
> 
> ```text
> shared supporting workstream
> ```
> 
> а не отдельный Program всегда.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20180. Program synthesis не должен механически создавать Program на каждую область.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20181. Принцип:
> 
> ```text
> Create separate Program
> only when coordination boundary matters.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20182. Coordination boundary может возникнуть из:
> 
> ```text
> distinct outcomes
> different governance
> different timelines
> different teams
> different risk profiles
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20183. Project Boundary
> 
> Аналогично Project должен существовать,
> 
> если есть отдельный:
> 
> ```text
> deliverable
> owner
> workflow
> verification
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20184. Не дробить систему на сотни искусственных Projects.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20185. Over-Decomposition Anti-Pattern
> 
> ```text
> one Action = one Project
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20186. Это создаёт administrative explosion.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20187. Under-Decomposition Anti-Pattern
> 
> ```text
> one gigantic Project
> ```
> 
> с 10 000 независимых задач.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20188. Program compiler ищет естественные boundaries.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20189. Boundary Detection
> 
> Signals:
> 
> ```text
> cohesive capability bundle
> shared deliverable
> shared resource set
> strong internal dependencies
> weak external coupling
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20190. Это напоминает:
> 
> ```text
> graph partitioning
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20191. Но final decomposition не должен быть purely algorithmic.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20192. LLM/graph partitioner может предложить.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20193. Governance/Program owner утверждает structure при необходимости.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20194. Program Graph
> 
> Nodes:
> 
> ```text
> Programs
> Projects
> Milestones
> Decisions
> Deliverables
> Capabilities
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20195. Relations:
> 
> ```text
> PART_OF
> DEPENDS_ON
> REQUIRES
> PRODUCES
> BLOCKS
> ENABLES
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20196. Example
> 
> ```text
> Sensor Research
> PRODUCES
> Sensor Prototype
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20197.
> 
> ```text
> Robot Integration
> REQUIRES
> Sensor Prototype
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20198. Это создаёт explicit dependency.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20199. Project Dependency Types
> 
> Не все dependencies одинаковы.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20200. Minimum:
> 
> ```text
> OUTPUT_DEPENDENCY
> CAPABILITY_DEPENDENCY
> RESOURCE_DEPENDENCY
> DECISION_DEPENDENCY
> KNOWLEDGE_DEPENDENCY
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20201. OUTPUT_DEPENDENCY
> 
> Project B требует Artifact from A.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20202. CAPABILITY_DEPENDENCY
> 
> B не может начать,
> 
> пока Capability C не operational.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20203. RESOURCE_DEPENDENCY
> 
> A и B используют один scarce Resource.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20204. DECISION_DEPENDENCY
> 
> Project cannot proceed before:
> 
> ```text
> Go/No-Go Decision
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20205. KNOWLEDGE_DEPENDENCY
> 
> B зависит от результата исследования A.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20206. Это особенно важно:
> 
> ```text
> Knowledge Dependency ≠ Schedule Dependency.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20207. Example Research Project заканчивается через 3 месяца,
> 
> но downstream engineering может начать раньше:
> 
> ```text
> with uncertainty
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20208. Поэтому dependency может быть:
> 
> ```text
> HARD
> SOFT
> CONDITIONAL
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20209. HARD
> 
> Не начинать до completion.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20210. SOFT
> 
> Можно начинать,
> 
> но риск rework.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20211. CONDITIONAL
> 
> Зависит от конкретного outcome.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20212. Example
> 
> Если sensor latency:
> 
> ```text
> <= 10 ms
> ```
> 
> используем architecture A.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20213. Иначе:
> 
> ```text
> architecture B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20214. Это не просто dependency.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20215. Это:
> 
> # Branching Program Logic
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20216. Program graph therefore может содержать:
> 
> ```text
> decision gates
> scenario branches
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20217. Program Gate
> 
> Gate — milestone + Decision criteria.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20218. Example:
> 
> ```text
> GATE 1:
> Is optical tactile sensing viable?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20219. Required evidence:
> 
> ```text
> latency test
> durability test
> signal quality
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20220. Possible Decisions:
> 
> ```text
> CONTINUE
> ITERATE
> PIVOT
> STOP
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20221. Gate ≠ arbitrary management checkpoint.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20222. Он должен быть связан с:
> 
> ```text
> uncertainty reduction
> commitment increase
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20223. Principle:
> 
> ```text
> Large irreversible commitment
> should usually follow stronger evidence.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20224. Это Adaptive Strategy integration.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20225. Stage-Gate без бюрократии
> 
> Traditional stage-gate может быть тяжёлым.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20226. Innovation OS делает gates:
> 
> ```text
> evidence-driven
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20227. Gate возникает где:
> 
> ```text
> decision consequence
> ```
> 
> значительна.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20228. Low-risk work не требует лишних gates.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20229. Example software prototype:
> 
> ```text
> automatic continuation
> ```
> 
> при проходящих tests.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20230. Example purchase €500k machine:
> 
> ```text
> explicit approval gate
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20231. Commitment Ladder
> 
> ```text
> Explore
> ↓
> Prototype
> ↓
> Pilot
> ↓
> Deploy
> ↓
> Scale
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20232. Каждый уровень увеличивает:
> 
> ```text
> resources
> lock-in
> organizational impact
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20233. Program compiler может предложить такую ladder.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20234. Program Baseline
> 
> После утверждения:
> 
> ```text
> program.lock
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20235. Contains:
> 
> ```text
> Programs
> Projects
> Dependencies
> Milestones
> Gate Criteria
> Critical Resource Commitments
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20236. Но Program execution динамический.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20237. Lock = baseline,
> 
> не rigid frozen schedule.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20238. Actual World State меняется.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20239. Program Control сравнивает:
> 
> ```text
> baseline
> vs
> actual
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20240. Это создаёт:
> 
> ```text
> Program Drift
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20241. Drift types:
> 
> ```text
> SCHEDULE
> SCOPE
> ARCHITECTURE
> RESOURCE
> BUDGET
> EVIDENCE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20242. Schedule Drift
> 
> Milestone позже baseline.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20243. Scope Drift
> 
> Requirements changed.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20244. Architecture Drift
> 
> Implementation diverges from architecture.lock.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20245. Resource Drift
> 
> Critical resource unavailable/replaced.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20246. Budget Drift
> 
> Cost assumptions changed.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20247. Evidence Drift
> 
> Previously accepted evidence invalidated.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20248. Program Drift ≠ failure.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20249. It means:
> 
> ```text
> current reality differs from plan
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20250. System then asks:
> 
> ```text
> Does this difference require adaptation?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20251. Program State Estimation
> 
> Program status should not be:
> 
> ```text
> green / yellow / red
> ```
> 
> only.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20252. Better dimensional state:
> 
> ```text
> schedule
> resource
> technical
> evidence
> budget
> governance
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20253. Example:
> 
> ```yaml
> schedule: healthy
> technical: uncertain
> budget: healthy
> resource: constrained
> evidence: insufficient
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20254. Это намного полезнее one-color dashboard.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20255. Mission Progress
> 
> Нельзя просто считать:
> 
> ```text
> Tasks Done / Tasks Total
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20256. Потому что 90% trivial tasks могут быть done,
> 
> но critical experiment unresolved.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20257. Better:
> 
> ```text
> Outcome Progress
> Evidence Progress
> Capability Progress
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20258. Outcome Progress
> 
> Какие required outcomes получены?
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20259. Capability Progress
> 
> Какие capabilities operational?
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20260. Evidence Progress
> 
> Какие critical Claims verified?
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20261. Milestone ≠ progress percentage.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20262. Program State can answer:
> 
> ```text
> What still prevents Mission completion?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20263. Mission Blocker
> 
> Derived view.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20264. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Tactile sensor prototype exists
> but durability evidence missing.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20265. Поэтому blocker:
> 
> ```text
> DURABILITY_VERIFICATION_GAP
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20266. Program Critical Path
> 
> Classic Critical Path Method полезен,
> 
> но недостаточен.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20267. Потому что innovation programs имеют:
> 
> ```text
> uncertain durations
> branching outcomes
> research failures
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20268. Поэтому нужен:
> 
> # Dynamic Critical Dependency Set
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20269. Это список элементов,
> 
> которые сейчас ограничивают:
> 
> ```text
> next major outcome
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20270. Example today:
> 
> ```text
> sensor experiment
> ```
> 
> critical.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20271. Tomorrow, после успеха:
> 
> ```text
> manufacturing slot
> ```
> 
> critical.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20272. Dynamic bottleneck changes.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20273. Program scheduler должен пересчитывать.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20274. Traditional Critical Path всё ещё можно использовать для deterministic segments.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20275. Но research dependency требует:
> 
> ```text
> conditional planning
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20276. Uncertain Task Duration
> 
> Represent:
> 
> ```text
> range
> ```
> 
> или distribution if evidence exists.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20277. Example:
> 
> ```text
> 2–6 weeks
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20278. Не:
> 
> ```text
> 4.000 weeks
> ```
> 
> fake precision.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20279. Program schedule can show:
> 
> ```text
> earliest
> likely range
> latest acceptable
> ```
> 
> where useful.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20280. But do not invent probability distributions without data.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20281. Research Project Outcomes
> 
> May include:
> 
> ```text
> SUCCESS
> PARTIAL
> REFUTED
> INCONCLUSIVE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20282. `REFUTED`
> 
> can be successful Project outcome scientifically.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20283. Example experiment goal:
> 
> ```text
> test hypothesis
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20284. Hypothesis refuted,
> 
> Project succeeded.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20285. Important invariant:
> 
> ```text
> Scientific Project Success
> ≠
> Hypothesis Confirmation.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20286. Program planner must handle negative results.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20287. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Fiber tactile route fails.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20288. Program does not automatically fail.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20289. Branch:
> 
> ```text
> capacitive skin alternative
> ```
> 
> opens.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20290. This is:
> 
> # Adaptive Program Branching
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20291. Preplanned Option
> 
> Strategy may already keep:
> 
> ```text
> Option A
> Option B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20292. If A fails,
> 
> B activated.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20293. This reduces replanning latency.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20294. But keeping options has cost.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20295. Example second sensor architecture may need:
> 
> ```text
> small parallel research investment
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20296. Option Value Engine decides whether preserving backup is worthwhile.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20297. Portfolio-level Resource Allocation
> 
> Several Projects compete for:
> 
> ```text
> money
> people
> GPU
> lab
> machine
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20298. Resource allocation is not just scheduling.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20299. It is:
> 
> ```text
> strategic allocation of scarce capabilities
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20300. Example
> 
> One photonics expert needed by:
> 
> ```text
> Sensor Project
> Calibration Project
> Manufacturing Project
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20301. Scheduler detects conflict.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20302. Options:
> 
> ```text
> sequence work
> train second person
> external partner
> automate part
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20303. Program engine invokes Capability Resolver.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20304. Resource Conflict Object
> 
> Derived:
> 
> ```text
> resource
> competing demands
> time overlap
> priority context
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20305. Priority cannot be arbitrary agent output.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20306. It comes from:
> 
> ```text
> Mission policy
> Gate urgency
> Safety
> Commitments
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20307. Example safety validation may take precedence over:
> 
> ```text
> optional feature work
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20308. But Program engine should explain allocation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20309. Resource Reservation
> 
> For scarce resources:
> 
> ```text
> lab slot
> machine
> specialist
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20310. Future reservation handled by Resource Market.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20311. Runtime scheduling handles immediate execution.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20312. Program engine coordinates both horizons.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20313. Multi-Horizon Planning
> 
> ```text
> Strategic:
> months/years
> 
> Program:
> weeks/months
> 
> Runtime:
> seconds/days
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20314. Same World State,
> 
> different planning resolution.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20315. Avoid one giant scheduler for everything.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20316. Hierarchical Planning
> 
> ```text
> Mission Planner
> ↓
> Program Planner
> ↓
> Project Compiler
> ↓
> Procedural Graph
> ↓
> Runtime Scheduler
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20317. Each layer resolves appropriate abstraction.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20318. Lower layer cannot silently modify higher-level Goal.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20319. Example Runtime can retry:
> 
> ```text
> Node B instead of A
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20320. But cannot decide:
> 
> ```text
> abandon tactile sensing strategy
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20321. That is strategic/program decision.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20322. Autonomy Boundary
> 
> Very important.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20323. Tactical adaptation
> 
> Examples:
> 
> ```text
> retry
> rebind provider
> move schedule within slack
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20324. Can be preauthorized.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20325. Strategic adaptation
> 
> Examples:
> 
> ```text
> change architecture
> cancel project
> shift mission scope
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20326. Requires higher governance.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20327. Program Policy defines:
> 
> ```text
> what changes are tactical
> what changes are strategic
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20328. Example schedule shift:
> 
> ```text
> < 3 days
> ```
> 
> might be tactical in one program,
> 
> strategic in another.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20329. Therefore threshold context-specific.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20330. Program Replanning
> 
> Trigger events:
> 
> ```text
> Project delayed
> Critical resource lost
> Experiment refuted hypothesis
> Budget changed
> New technology appears
> Standard changed
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20331. Replanning pipeline
> 
> ```text
> Event
> ↓
> Impact Analysis
> ↓
> Affected Dependencies
> ↓
> Alternative Paths
> ↓
> Replan Proposal
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20332. Replanning should be incremental.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20333. Do not recompute entire world for every minor Event.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20334. Dependency graph identifies affected subgraph.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20335. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Sensor supplier delay
> ```
> 
> affects:
> 
> ```text
> sensor integration
> benchmark
> pilot
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20336. Unrelated:
> 
> ```text
> funding documentation
> ```
> 
> continues.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20337. This is incremental program propagation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20338. Program Impact Analysis
> 
> For any change:
> 
> ```text
> what Projects?
> what milestones?
> what Decisions?
> what commitments?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20339. Example Architecture Change:
> 
> ```text
> cloud model → local model
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20340. Impact:
> 
> ```text
> GPU procurement
> benchmark
> privacy review
> deployment workflow
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20341. System generates affected Work Package.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20342. Replanning Proposal
> 
> Contains:
> 
> ```text
> reason
> affected baseline
> new dependencies
> resource impact
> unknowns
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20343. Proposal ≠ new baseline.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20344. Governance approves if strategic.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20345. Then:
> 
> ```text
> program.lock v2
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20346. Baseline History
> 
> ```text
> v1
> v2
> v3
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20347. Preserve why changed.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20348. Program Time Travel
> 
> Can reconstruct:
> 
> ```text
> what plan existed on date T?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20349. Useful for audit and learning.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20350. Workstream
> 
> Useful application abstraction.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20351. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Sensing Workstream
> AI Workstream
> Hardware Workstream
> Validation Workstream
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20352. Workstream may cut across Projects.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20353. Поэтому не новый root.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20354. It is:
> 
> ```text
> View/Context grouping
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20355. Workstreams improve human navigation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20356. Package/Work Breakdown Structure
> 
> Traditional WBS useful,
> 
> but should be generated from semantic dependencies.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20357. Not manually numbered hierarchy only.
>

> # Capability Capital, Ecosystem Learning & Technological Development Accounting v0.1
> 
> ## 20789. Главный переход
> 
> До сих пор Innovation OS измерял в основном:
> 
> ```text
> Projects
> Actions
> Artifacts
> Costs
> Events
> ```
> 
> Но для Virtual Technopark этого недостаточно.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20790. Главный долгосрочный вопрос
> 
> Не:
> 
> ```text
> Сколько Projects завершено?
> ```
> 
> а:
> 
> ```text
> Что система теперь умеет делать
> такого,
> чего раньше не умела?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20791. Это и есть переход к
> 
> # Capability Capital
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20792. Capability Capital
> 
> Можно определить как:
> 
> > совокупность доступных, доказанных, воспроизводимых и организационно удерживаемых возможностей экосистемы создавать результаты определённого класса.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20793. Ключевые слова здесь:
> 
> ```text
> available
> evidenced
> reproducible
> retained
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20794. Поэтому наличие Resource ещё не означает Capability Capital.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20795. Example
> 
> Организация купила:
> 
> ```text
> industrial robot
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20796. Но:
> 
> ```text
> нет trained operator
> нет programming workflow
> нет safety procedure
> нет fixture
> нет verification
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20797. Следовательно:
> 
> ```text
> Robot Resource exists
> ```
> 
> но:
> 
> ```text
> Robotic Manipulation Capability
> ```
> 
> может быть:
> 
> ```text
> NOT_OPERATIONAL
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20798. Другой пример
> 
> Один инженер умеет:
> 
> ```text
> настраивать редкую систему
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20799. Пока знание существует только у него:
> 
> ```text
> Capability exists
> ```
> 
> но она:
> 
> ```text
> PERSON_BOUND
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20800. Если инженер недоступен:
> 
> ```text
> Capability effectively unavailable.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20801. Поэтому Capability Capital должен учитывать
> 
> ```text
> не только наличие знания,
> но и его устойчивость.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20802. Capability Retention Classes
> 
> Предлагаются:
> 
> ```text
> PERSON_BOUND
> TEAM_BOUND
> RESOURCE_BOUND
> ORGANIZATIONAL
> INSTITUTIONALIZED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20803. PERSON_BOUND
> 
> Capability зависит критически от:
> 
> ```text
> одного конкретного человека
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20804. Example
> 
> ```text
> only Alice knows

> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20805. TEAM_BOUND
> 
> Знание распределено между:

> 
> # 20806. Оно устойчивее,
> 
> но может исчезнуть при распаде команды.

> ---
> 
> # 20807. RESOURCE_BOUND
> 
> Capability существует только пока доступен:

> 
> # 20808. Example

> # 20815. Example

> # 20816. Поэтому Capital динамический.

> 
> Для Capability C:

> Providers

> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20872. Capability Capital Graph
> 
> ```text
> Capability
> ├── Providers
> ├── Procedures
> ├── Evidence
> ├── Dependencies
> ├── Training
> └── Operational Uses
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20873. Example
> 
> ```text
> LOCAL_LLM_INFERENCE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20874. Providers:
> 
> ```text
> GPU Node A
> ARM Node B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20875. Procedures:
> 
> ```text
> deployment package
> model loading workflow
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20876. Evidence:
> 
> ```text
> latency benchmark
> quality evaluation
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20877. Dependencies:
> 
> ```text
> runtime
> drivers
> models
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20878. Training:
> 
> ```text
> operator guide
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20879. Operational Uses:
> 
> ```text
> Research Program
> Document Pipeline
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20880. Чем больше связей устойчиво закрыты,
> 
> тем более institutionalized Capability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20881. But do not infer maturity from graph density alone.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20882. One high-quality procedure may be better than:
> 
> ```text
> 20 obsolete documents
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20883. Evidence quality matters.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20884. Reproducibility
> 
> Capability reusable only if:
> 
> ```text
> another execution
> can produce expected outcome
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20885. Reproducibility evidence can come from:
> 
> ```text
> repeated runs
> independent provider
> independent team
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20886. Levels:
> 
> ```text
> SINGLE_DEMONSTRATION
> REPEATED_SAME_PROVIDER
> REPEATED_DIFFERENT_OPERATOR
> REPEATED_DIFFERENT_PROVIDER
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20887. Последний даёт stronger evidence of portability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20888. Но не обязательно нужен для каждой Capability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20889. Example:
> 
> ```text
> unique telescope
> ```
> 
> может не иметь second provider.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20890. Capability всё равно valuable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20891. Просто:
> 
> ```text
> provider concentration = high
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20892. Capability Concentration Risk
> 
> Если одна Capability зависит от:
> 
> ```text
> 1 person
> 1 machine
> 1 vendor
> 1 site
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20893. System exposes:
> 
> ```text
> single-provider dependency
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20894. Это не обязательно проблема.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20895. Но если Capability critical:
> 
> может стать strategic risk.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20896. Criticality Context
> 
> Capability may be critical for:
> 
> ```text
> Mission A
> ```
> 
> и irrelevant для:
> 
> ```text
> Mission B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20897. Поэтому:
> 
> ```text
> criticality
> ```
> 
> не global intrinsic property.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20898. It derives from:
> 
> ```text
> active dependency graph
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20899. Example
> 
> ```text
> CNC machining
> ```
> 
> может быть critical this month,
> 
> but not after prototype phase.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20900. Dynamic Capability Criticality
> 
> Mission Control вычисляет:
> 
> ```text
> which current capabilities
> block important outcomes
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20901. Capital view затем показывает:
> 
> ```text
> critical + fragile
> ```
> 
> capabilities.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20902. Это особенно полезный quadrant.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20903. Four-way view
> 
> ```text
> Critical + Resilient
> Critical + Fragile
> Noncritical + Resilient
> Noncritical + Fragile
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20904. Не как оценка «хорошо/плохо»,
> 
> а как management view.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20905. Critical + Fragile
> 
> Может требовать:
> 
> ```text
> redundancy
> training
> documentation
> alternative provider
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20906. Capability Fragility
> 
> Dimensions:
> 
> ```text
> provider concentration
> documentation gaps
> maintenance gaps
> external dependency
> knowledge concentration
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20907. Example
> 
> Capability technically verified,
> 
> но:
> 
> ```text
> only one undocumented script
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20908. Fragile.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20909. Institutionalization Path
> 
> ```text
> Person Knowledge
> ↓
> Documented Procedure
> ↓
> Executable Package
> ↓
> Verification Suite
> ↓
> Multiple Operators
> ↓
> Multiple Providers
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20910. Not every Capability needs final stage.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20911. Example rare research technique
> 
> might reasonably remain:
> 
> ```text
> expert-bound
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20912. Institutionalization should depend on:
> 
> ```text
> frequency
> criticality
> transfer value
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20913. Opportunity Engine can identify:
> 
> ```text
> institutionalization opportunity
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20914. Example repeated dependence on one expert.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20915. Candidate actions:
> 
> ```text
> document procedure
> train backup
> automate part
> create package
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20916. This is another form of innovation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20917. Knowledge Capital
> 
> Capability often depends on:
> 
> ```text
> Know-What
> Know-How
> Know-Why
> Know-Who
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20918. Know-What
> 
> Facts, specifications.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20919. Know-How
> 
> Procedures.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20920. Know-Why
> 
> Models, causal understanding.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20921. Know-Who
> 
> Where expertise/resources reside.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20922. Technopark needs all four.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20923. Example
> 
> You may know:
> 
> ```text
> which sensor exists
> ```
> 
> but not:
> 
> ```text
> how to integrate it.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20924. Capability incomplete.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20925. Knowledge objects remain:
> 
> ```text
> Claims
> Artifacts
> Evidence
> Concepts
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20926. No Knowledge root required.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20927. Procedural Knowledge
> 
> Especially important.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20928. Procedure may start as:
> 
> ```text
> human notes
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20929. Then become:
> 
> ```text
> structured workflow
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20930. Then:
> 
> ```text
> Procedural Graph
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20931. Then:
> 
> ```text
> tested Capability Package
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20932. This is:
> 
> # Knowledge Operationalization Pipeline
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20933. Formula
> 
> ```text
> Tacit Knowledge
> ↓
> Explicit Artifact
> ↓
> Structured Procedure
> ↓
> Executable Workflow
> ↓
> Verified Capability
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20934. Not every tacit skill can fully formalize.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20935. Example manual craftsmanship.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20936. Тогда system может retain:
> 
> ```text
> human skill provider
> +
> documentation
> +
> training
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20937. Important:
> 
> ```text
> Institutionalization ≠ Full Automation.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20938. Human capability can be institutionalized through:
> 
> ```text
> training
> standards
> multiple practitioners
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20939. Capability Transferability
> 
> Question:
> 
> ```text
> Can capability move
> to another team/site/node?
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20940. Transfer types:
> 
> ```text
> SOFTWARE_PORTABLE
> PROCEDURE_PORTABLE
> TRAINING_TRANSFERABLE
> EQUIPMENT_DEPENDENT
> SITE_BOUND
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20941. Example software package:
> 
> high portability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20942. Example clean-room process:
> 
> site-dependent.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20943. Example specialist expertise:
> 
> training-transferable with time.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20944. Transferability matters for federation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20945. Federated Capability Capital
> 
> Organization A may provide Capability to B.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20946. B does not necessarily own capability internally.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20947. Distinguish:
> 
> ```text
> INTERNAL_CAPABILITY
> FEDERATED_ACCESS
> MARKET_ACCESS
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20948. Example:
> 
> ```text
> electron microscope
> ```
> 
> available through partner lab.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20949. Project can use it.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20950. But internal Capability Capital differs.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20951. Because access can disappear.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20952. Thus:
> 
> ```text
> Access ≠ Ownership.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20953. Another important distinction:
> 
> ```text
> Ownership ≠ Operational Capability.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20954. You may own machine
> 
> without knowing how to use it.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20955. Capability Access Modes
> 
> ```text
> OWNED_INTERNAL
> SHARED_INTERNAL
> FEDERATED
> COMMERCIAL
> TEMPORARY
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20956. These help resilience/planning.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20957. But avoid value judgement.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20958. External capability may be perfectly sufficient.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20959. Capability Sovereignty
> 
> Some Missions require:
> 
> ```text
> local control
> local data
> strategic autonomy
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20960. Then external-only Capability may not satisfy policy.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20961. Strategy can create:
> 
> ```text
> Capability Sovereignty Requirement
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20962. Example:
> 
> ```text
> must be operable without external cloud.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20963. This becomes Constraint.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20964. Capital Accounting therefore should show:
> 
> ```text
> internal
> external
> contingent
> ```
> 
> availability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20965. Capability Dependency Graph
> 
> Capability A may require:
> 
> ```text
> Capability B
> Capability C
> Resource D
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20966. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Tactile Robot Control
> ```
> 
> requires:
> 
> ```text
> Tactile Sensing
> Realtime Inference
> Robot Motion Control
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20967. Higher-order Capability Capital is therefore:
> 
> ```text
> compositional.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20968. If lower capability lost:
> 
> ```text
> higher capability may degrade.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20969. This requires dependency propagation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20970. Capability Failure Propagation
> 
> Event:
> 
> ```text
> GPU Node unavailable
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20971. Direct Capability:
> 
> ```text
> LOCAL_GPU_INFERENCE
> ```
> 
> becomes unavailable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20972. Dependent:
> 
> ```text
> LOCAL_DOCUMENT_ANALYSIS
> ```
> 
> may become degraded.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20973. But if alternate ARM provider exists:
> 
> ```text
> capability remains available
> ```
> 
> with lower performance.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20974. Capital graph must support:
> 
> ```text
> alternative provider paths.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20975. This resembles resilience graph.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20976. Capability Availability is derived,
> 
> not static property.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20977. It depends on:
> 
> ```text
> providers
> resources
> dependencies
> constraints
> context
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20978. Example capability available:
> 
> ```text
> in Dresden lab
> ```
> 
> but not:
> 
> ```text
> remote/mobile context.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20979. Capability availability must therefore be:
> 
> ```text
> Context-sensitive.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20980. Global statement:
> 
> ```text
> "We have Capability X"
> ```
> 
> is often too coarse.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20981. Better:
> 
> ```text
> Capability X is operational
> for Context C
> under Contract V
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20982. This is core precision.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20983. Capability Capital Unit
> 
> No single numerical unit.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20984. Capital is graph/state,
> 
> not scalar.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20985. Yet aggregate reporting useful.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20986. Example dashboard:
> 
> ```text
> New Verified Capabilities: 12
> Capabilities Lost: 2
> Person-Bound Critical Capabilities: 4
> Reusable Packages Produced: 8
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20987. These counts are descriptive.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20988. Trend:
> 
> ```text
> person-bound → institutionalized
> ```
> 
> can be useful.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20989. Institutionalization Rate
> 
> Could count:
> 
> ```text
> how many critical capabilities
> moved to more resilient retention states.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20990. But not performance target blindly.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20991. Some capability should remain specialist.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20992. Capability Portfolio
> 
> Similar to Project portfolio.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20993. Clusters:
> 
> ```text
> software
> research
> physical
> organizational
> human
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20994. Example capability domains:
> 
> ```text
> AI
> Photonics
> Robotics
> Manufacturing
> Funding
> Legal
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20995. Capability Map
> 
> 2D graph:
> 
> ```text
> Capabilities
> ↔ Providers
> ↔ Projects
> ↔ Evidence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20996. High-level semantic zoom:
> 
> ```text
> domain capability clusters
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20997. Drill down:
> 
> ```text
> individual provider
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20998. Capability Landscape
> 
> Can show:
> 
> ```text
> Strong Coverage
> Sparse Coverage
> Single-Provider Areas
> Emerging Areas
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 20999. But avoid calling one cluster «weak» solely because small.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21000. Major milestone
> 
> К **21000** Virtual Technopark начинает учитывать:
> 
> # Capability Capital
> 
> не как список оборудования,
> 
> а как:
> 
> ```text
> verified ability
> +
> knowledge
> +
> providers
> +
> procedures
> +
> resilience
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21001. Capability Gap Accounting
> 
> Capital view also shows:
> 
> ```text
> missing capabilities
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21002. But gap categories:
> 
> ```text
> ABSENT
> UNVERIFIED
> UNAVAILABLE
> FRAGILE
> INSUFFICIENT_CAPACITY
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21003. ABSENT
> 
> No known provider.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21004. UNVERIFIED
> 
> Provider exists,
> 
> evidence inadequate.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21005. UNAVAILABLE
> 
> Normally exists,
> 
> currently inaccessible.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21006. FRAGILE
> 
> Exists,
> 
> but single point of failure.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21007. INSUFFICIENT_CAPACITY
> 
> Capability exists,
> 
> but quantity/time insufficient.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21008. Эти distinctions critically affect response.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21009. Example ABSENT:
> 
> ```text
> research/build
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21010. UNVERIFIED:
> 
> ```text
> benchmark/test
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21011. UNAVAILABLE:
> 
> ```text
> reschedule/provider switch
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21012. FRAGILE:
> 
> ```text
> redundancy/training
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21013. INSUFFICIENT_CAPACITY:
> 
> ```text
> scale/share/procure
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21014. Capability Debt
> 
> Теперь важное понятие.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21015. Capability Debt
> 
> Можно определить как:
> 
> > структурная зависимость от хрупких, недокументированных, устаревших или трудно воспроизводимых способов предоставления необходимой Capability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21016. Примеры:
> 
> ```text
> single undocumented script
> one expert
> unsupported library
> obsolete machine
> manual fragile workflow
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21017. Capability Debt ≠ Technical Debt only.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21018. Потому что может быть:
> 
> ```text
> human
> organizational
> physical
> knowledge
> ```
> 
> debt.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21019. Debt classes:
> 
> ```text
> KNOWLEDGE_DEBT
> AUTOMATION_DEBT
> INFRASTRUCTURE_DEBT
> STANDARDIZATION_DEBT
> VERIFICATION_DEBT
> SUCCESSION_DEBT
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21020. KNOWLEDGE_DEBT
> 
> Capability works,
> 
> but know-how poorly documented.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21021. AUTOMATION_DEBT
> 
> Repeated process depends heavily on manual repetitive steps.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21022. INFRASTRUCTURE_DEBT
> 
> Capability depends on obsolete/fragile infrastructure.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21023. STANDARDIZATION_DEBT
> 
> Many incompatible local implementations.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21024. VERIFICATION_DEBT
> 
> Capability widely assumed,
> 
> but evidence outdated/missing.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21025. SUCCESSION_DEBT
> 
> Knowledge concentrated in:
> 
> ```text
> one person / one small team
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21026. Debt is not automatically bad.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21027. Early research prototype naturally has:
> 
> ```text
> high debt
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21028. It becomes problem if:
> 
> ```text
> capability becomes critical
> ```
> 
> but debt remains.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21029. Therefore debt significance:
> 
> ```text
> Debt × Contextual Criticality
> ```
> 
> conceptually.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21030. Again avoid arbitrary numeric multiplication if not justified.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21031. Debt Remediation Options
> 
> ```text
> document
> train
> standardize
> replace
> automate
> add provider
> reverify
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21032. Each remediation may become:
> 
> ```text
> Project
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21033. Opportunity Engine can generate:
> 
> ```text
> Capability Hardening Opportunity
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21034. Hardening
> 
> Means:
> 
> ```text
> make capability more robust/repeatable
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21035. Example:
> 
> ```text
> Prototype OCR pipeline
> ```
> 
> →
> 
> ```text
> documented package
> automated tests
> ARM/x86 providers
> monitoring
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21036. Same nominal Capability,
> 
> much greater Capital quality.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21037. Capability Hardening Pipeline
> 
> ```text
> Demonstrate
> ↓
> Document
> ↓
> Test
> ↓
> Package
> ↓
> Replicate
> ↓
> Monitor
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21038. Not mandatory all at once.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21039. Capability Depreciation
> 
> Capital can decline over time.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21040. Not financial depreciation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21041. Causes:
> 
> ```text
> software obsolescence
> expert attrition
> equipment aging
> standard incompatibility
> data drift
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21042. Example model performance degrades because:
> 
> ```text
> environment changes
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21043. Capability state:
> 
> ```text
> OPERATIONAL → DEGRADED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21044. Periodic verification can detect.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21045. Capability Freshness
> 
> Evidence age matters.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21046. Example benchmark from:
> 
> ```text
> 3 years ago
> ```
> 
> may not represent current deployment.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21047. But age alone does not invalidate.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21048. Reverification trigger can depend on:
> 
> ```text
> component change
> environment change
> standard change
> time
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21049. Time-based reverification only where justified.
>

> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21778. Complete self-sufficiency is costly.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21779. Extreme specialization can be fragile.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21780. Ecosystem analysis should expose both.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21781. Specialization Index
> 
> Could be descriptive based on:
> 
> ```text
> capability concentration by provider
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21782. But do not create social ranking.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21783. Purpose:
> 
> ```text
> identify dependency structure
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21784. Complementarity
> 
> Two providers are complementary if:
> 
> ```text
> their capabilities jointly satisfy
> frequent requirement bundles
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21785. Example
> 
> ```text
> sensor manufacturing
> +
> signal processing
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21786. Complementarity can be learned from:
> 
> ```text
> Project co-occurrence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21787. But repeated co-occurrence ≠ causal necessity.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21788. Semantic contracts can verify actual requirement linkage.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21789. Complementarity Graph
> 
> Edges weighted/described by:
> 
> ```text
> joint usage frequency
> shared project count
> dependency relation
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21790. This can reveal:
> 
> ```text
> latent consortium opportunities
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21791. Example
> 
> Three organizations repeatedly provide:
> 
> ```text
> hardware
> software
> validation
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21792. System may propose:
> 
> ```text
> reusable consortium archetype
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21793. Candidate Consortium ≠ Organization.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21794. Existing Dynamic Organization module handles formalization.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21795. Knowledge Diffusion
> 
> Knowledge can spread via:
> 
> ```text
> papers
> code
> training
> joint projects
> person movement
> standards
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21796. But each channel has different semantics.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21797. Paper access may transfer:
> 
> ```text
> Know-What
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21798. Joint project may transfer:
> 
> ```text
> Know-How
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21799. Training can transfer:
> 
> ```text
> operational skill
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21800. Code package can transfer:
> 
> ```text
> partial executable know-how
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21801. Therefore diffusion must distinguish:
> 
> ```text
> INFORMATION
> PROCEDURE
> CAPABILITY
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21802. Critical invariant:
> 
> ```text
> Information Diffusion
> ≠
> Capability Diffusion.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21803. Example
> 
> 100 labs download procedure.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21804. Only 3 reproduce result.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21805. Information diffused widely.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21806. Capability diffused narrowly.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21807. Capability Diffusion Event
> 
> Requires evidence that:
> 
> ```text
> new provider successfully performs capability.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21808. Knowledge Transfer Chain
> 
> ```text
> Source
> ↓
> Artifact/Training
> ↓
> Recipient
> ↓
> Attempt
> ↓
> Verification
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21809. Only after verification:
> 
> ```text
> Capability Provider added.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21810. Diffusion Friction
> 
> Factors may include:
> 
> ```text
> complexity
> equipment dependency
> documentation
> training time
> legal restrictions
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21811. Example software package:
> 
> low replication friction.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21812. Example advanced surgery technique:
> 
> high replication friction.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21813. Innovation OS should not treat both equally.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21814. Diffusion Path
> 
> Can be:
> 
> ```text
> direct
> through broker
> through package
> through training center
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21815. Example
> 
> ```text
> Lab A
> → Standard Procedure
> → Labs B/C/D
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21816. Standard acts as:
> 
> ```text
> diffusion infrastructure
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21817. Technology Diffusion
> 
> A technology may move through adoption stages.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21818. Potential states:
> 
> ```text
> DISCOVERED
> EVALUATING
> PILOTING
> ADOPTED
> OPERATIONAL
> RETIRED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21819. These states belong per organization/context.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21820. Global technology does not have one universal adoption state.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21821. Example
> 
> Technology X:
> 
> ```text
> Lab A = operational
> Company B = piloting
> Organization C = rejected
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21822. This is normal.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21823. Adoption ≠ success.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21824. Some adopted technologies later fail.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21825. Technology Adoption Event
> 
> ```text
> TECHNOLOGY_PILOT_STARTED
> TECHNOLOGY_ADOPTED
> TECHNOLOGY_RETIRED
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21826. Adoption Reason
> 
> Could include:
> 
> ```text
> cost
> performance
> standardization
> availability
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21827. But motives should be based on:
> 
> ```text
> Decision records
> ```
> 
> not inferred psychologically.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21828. Technology Diffusion Map
> 
> Shows:
> 
> ```text
> which organizations use which technology
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21829. Combined with spatial map:
> 
> ```text
> geographic diffusion
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21830. But avoid:
> 
> ```text
> surveillance-like individual tracking
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21831. Organization/site level often sufficient.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21832. Innovation Diffusion Speed
> 
> Can measure:
> 
> ```text
> time between verified first use
> and subsequent independent adoption
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21833. Useful descriptive signal.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21834. But faster diffusion ≠ better technology.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21835. Marketing, regulation or standards can influence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21836. Therefore do not infer:
> 
> ```text
> fast diffusion = technically superior.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21837. Adoption Barrier Analysis
> 
> If strong capability remains rarely adopted,
> 
> possible barriers:
> 
> ```text
> cost
> integration
> skills
> standards
> trust
> regulation
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21838. These become:
> 
> ```text
> Hypotheses
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21839. Example
> 
> Open-source tool technically capable,
> 
> but adoption low.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21840. Could be because:
> 
> ```text
> deployment difficult
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21841. Opportunity:
> 
> ```text
> packaging / managed deployment
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21842. Technology Diffusion and Network Effects
> 
> Some capabilities become more valuable as adoption grows.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21843. Example:
> 
> ```text
> shared semantic protocol
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21844. More compatible nodes:
> 
> ```text
> more potential interactions
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21845. That's a network effect.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21846. But not all technologies have network effects.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21847. Example microscope performance does not directly increase because more laboratories own microscopes.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21848. Though shared protocols/data may produce indirect benefits.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21849. Network Effect Type
> 
> Could include:
> 
> ```text
> INTEROPERABILITY
> DATA
> MARKET_LIQUIDITY
> KNOWLEDGE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21850. INTEROPERABILITY
> 
> More nodes share same standard.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21851. DATA
> 
> More use generates:
> 
> ```text
> more datasets
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21852. MARKET_LIQUIDITY
> 
> More buyers/sellers improve matching.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21853. KNOWLEDGE
> 
> More practitioners produce:
> 
> ```text
> documentation
> bug fixes
> experience
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21854. But network effects can also create:
> 
> ```text
> lock-in
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21855. Path Dependence
> 
> Early choice can shape future ecosystem.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21856. Example
> 
> Standard A gets early adoption.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21857. More tools integrate A.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21858. Then switching becomes harder.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21859. This is:
> 
> ```text
> path dependence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21860. It does not mean A is technically optimal.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21861. Ecosystem memory should preserve:
> 
> ```text
> why adoption happened
> ```
> 
> where Decision evidence exists.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21862. Lock-In
> 
> Possible sources:
> 
> ```text
> proprietary interfaces
> data format
> skills
> contracts
> network effects
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21863. Lock-in is not inherently bad.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21864. It can buy:
> 
> ```text
> efficiency
> stability
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21865. But reduces switching options.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21866. Strategy Engine can model:
> 
> ```text
> switching path
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21867. Ecosystem Evolution must therefore track:
> 
> ```text
> optionality
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21868. Standard Competition
> 
> Multiple profiles may coexist.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21869. Example
> 
> ```text
> Protocol A
> Protocol B
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21870. Ecosystem may:
> 
> ```text
> converge
> remain plural
> use adapters
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21871. Do not automatically force convergence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21872. Semantic pluralism remains valid.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21873. Convergence Signal
> 
> Could be:
> 
> ```text
> increasing common adoption
> decreasing mapping cost
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21874. Fragmentation Signal
> 
> ```text
> many incompatible profiles
> many custom adapters
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21875. Opportunity Engine may propose:
> 
> ```text
> bridge standard
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21876. But standardization decision remains governance matter.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21877. Institution Formation
> 
> Repeated coordination sometimes produces:
> 
> ```text
> working group
> consortium
> foundation
> shared service
> standard body
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21878. These are institutional responses.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21879. Dynamic Organization Engine can detect:
> 
> ```text
> stable collaboration pattern
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21880. Opportunity Hypothesis:
> 
> ```text
> formal organization may reduce coordination cost
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21881. But:
> 
> ```text
> network stability
> ≠
> need for legal entity.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21882. Sometimes informal federation is better.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21883. Institution Formation Criteria
> 
> Potential signals:
> 
> ```text
> repeated shared decisions
> shared budget
> shared infrastructure
> shared liability
> long-term coordination
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21884. Different institutional forms can be proposed.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21885. Example
> 
> ```text
> informal working group
> shared service agreement
> consortium
> association
> company
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21886. Legal suitability depends on jurisdiction.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21887. Architecture layer should stay neutral.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21888. Institution ≠ Capability
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21889. But institution can:
> 
> ```text
> retain
> coordinate
> reproduce
> ```
> 
> Capabilities.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21890. Institutional Memory
> 
> Organization can outlive individual members.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21891. If:
> 
> ```text
> procedures
> roles
> data
> governance
> ```
> 
> are retained.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21892. This is why institution formation can increase Capability Capital.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21893. But institution can also add:
> 
> ```text
> bureaucratic overhead
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21894. Therefore not universally beneficial.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21895. Coordination Cost
> 
> Can be inferred from:
> 
> ```text
> delays
> repeated negotiations
> duplicated integration
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21896. Opportunity:
> 
> ```text
> new coordination mechanism
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21897. Examples:
> 
> ```text
> shared schema
> market
> scheduler
> working group
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21898. Different mechanisms solve different coordination problems.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21899. Ecosystem Market Formation
> 
> When repeated:
> 
> ```text
> Capability Demand
> ↔ Capability Supply
> ```
> 
> exists,
> 
> a market-like structure can emerge.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21900. Example
> 
> Projects repeatedly seek:
> 
> ```text
> GPU hours
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21901. Multiple providers offer:
> 
> ```text
> compute capacity
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21902. Capability Exchange becomes useful.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21903. Market Formation Stages
> 
> Descriptively:
> 
> ```text
> BILATERAL
> REPEATED_MATCHING
> SHARED_REGISTRY
> EXCHANGE
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21904. BILATERAL
> 
> Manual one-to-one agreements.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21905. REPEATED_MATCHING
> 
> Recurring demand/supply patterns.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21906. SHARED_REGISTRY
> 
> Offers/demands become discoverable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21907. EXCHANGE
> 
> Standard matching/reservation mechanisms.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21908. Not every capability should become market commodity.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21909. Example:
> 
> ```text
> high-trust strategic research collaboration
> ```
> 
> may remain relational.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21910. Therefore:
> 
> ```text
> Capability Market ≠ universal commodification.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21911. Capability Commoditization
> 
> Occurs when:
> 
> ```text
> interface stable
> providers substitutable
> quality measurable
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21912. Example generic compute.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21913. Less commoditized:
> 
> ```text
> frontier research leadership
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21914. System can describe degree of substitutability.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21915. Substitutability Graph
> 
> Requirement R can be satisfied by:
> 
> ```text
> Provider A
> Provider B
> Provider C
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21916. This reduces dependency.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21917. But if outputs vary significantly,
> 
> they may not be true substitutes.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21918. Semantic Contract ensures comparison.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21919. Capability Market Liquidity
> 
> Could measure:
> 
> ```text
> open demands
> available supplies
> match completion time
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21920. Useful diagnostically.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21921. Low liquidity can arise from:
> 
> ```text
> scarcity
> poor discovery
> incompatible contracts
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21922. Different problems need different interventions.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21923. Scarcity Propagation
> 
> A scarce Capability can constrain many downstream projects.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21924. Example:
> 
> ```text
> one chip fabrication slot
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21925. Projects queue.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21926. Demand signal propagates upward.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21927. Opportunity options:
> 
> ```text
> expand capacity
> find substitute
> redesign product
> reschedule
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21928. Ecosystem reacts.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21929. This resembles adaptive supply network.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21930. Supply Shock
> 
> Example:
> 
> ```text
> supplier disappears
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21931. Direct effects:
> 
> ```text
> Resource unavailable
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21932. Indirect effects:
> 
> ```text
> Capabilities degrade
> Projects block
> Programs replan
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21933. Ecosystem Stress Test
> 
> Scenario:
> 
> ```text
> remove supplier X
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21934. Compute:
> 
> ```text
> affected resources
> capabilities
> projects
> organizations
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21935. Another scenario:
> 
> ```text
> loss of cloud region
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21936. Another:
> 
> ```text
> lab site inaccessible
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21937. Another:
> 
> ```text
> semantic standard incompatible
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21938. This expands Capability Stress Testing to ecosystem level.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21939. Systemic Risk
> 
> Risk that local failure propagates widely.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21940. Example:
> 
> ```text
> single authentication provider
> ```
> 
> used across federation.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21941. Failure disables:
> 
> ```text
> many independent capabilities.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21942. Network analysis can find:
> 
> ```text
> systemic dependency nodes
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21943. But centrality alone ≠ systemic criticality.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21944. Need actual operational dependency.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21945. Dependency Cascade
> 
> ```text
> Resource Failure
> ↓
> Capability Loss
> ↓
> Project Blocking
> ↓
> Program Delay
> ↓
> Mission Impact
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21946. This cascade should be explainable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21947. Example output
> 
> ```text
> Node R failed
> → Capability C unavailable
> → Projects P1/P4 blocked
> → Mission M2 delayed
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21948. This is operationally actionable.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21949. Contagion vs Propagation
> 
> Avoid social metaphor overreach.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21950. Better technical term:
> 
> ```text
> dependency propagation
> ```
> 
> for infrastructure failures.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21951. Knowledge diffusion may be called diffusion.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21952. Failure spread should retain causal dependency semantics.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21953. Ecosystem Resilience
> 
> Dimensions:
> 
> ```text
> redundancy
> substitutability
> recovery
> distribution
> coordination
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21954. Do not reduce to one resilience score.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21955. Redundancy
> 
> Multiple equivalent resources.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21956. Substitutability
> 
> Different resources can satisfy same Requirement.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21957. Recovery
> 
> Lost capability can be restored.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21958. Distribution
> 
> Capabilities not all concentrated in one failure domain.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21959. Coordination
> 
> Network can reallocate work after disruption.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21960. Adaptive Resilience
> 
> More than backup.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21961. Example supplier lost.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21962. Ecosystem:
> 
> ```text
> discovers alternative
> rewrites architecture
> reroutes work
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21963. That is adaptive resilience.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21964. Static resilience:
> 
> ```text
> preexisting backup.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21965. Both useful.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21966. Recovery Capability itself is Capital.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21967. Example:
> 
> ```text
> ability to redeploy services
> to alternate nodes
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21968. It can be verified.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21969. Ecosystem Diversity
> 
> Can describe diversity of:
> 
> ```text
> technologies
> providers
> domains
> methods
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21970. Diversity may improve option value.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21971. But too much heterogeneity can increase:
> 
> ```text
> integration cost
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21972. Therefore again:
> 
> ```text
> diversity ≠ always better.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21973. Homogeneity gives:
> 
> ```text
> standardization efficiency
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21974. Diversity gives:
> 
> ```text
> alternative paths
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21975. Strategy chooses balance.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21976. Evolutionary Capability Development
> 
> Теперь можно использовать осторожную evolutionary analogy.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21977. Не биологический детерминизм.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21978. А инженерная схема:
> 
> ```text
> VARIATION
> SELECTION
> RETENTION
> RECOMBINATION
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21979. VARIATION
> 
> Создаются разные:
> 
> ```text
> architecture candidates
> methods
> packages
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21980. SELECTION
> 
> Некоторые проходят:
> 
> ```text
> tests
> constraints
> operational evaluation
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21981. RETENTION
> 
> Успешные варианты превращаются в:
> 
> ```text
> packages
> standards
> procedures
> capability capital
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21982. RECOMBINATION
> 
> Существующие Capabilities объединяются:
> 
> ```text
> в новые systems.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21983. Это даёт:
> 
> # Evolutionary Capability Loop
> 
> ```text
> variation
> ↓
> test
> ↓
> selection
> ↓
> retention
> ↓
> recombination
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21984. Важное ограничение
> 
> ```text
> Selection ≠ survival of the strongest.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21985. В инженерном контексте selection означает:
> 
> ```text
> variant retained because it satisfies
> specific requirements under evidence.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21986. Другой context может выбрать другой variant.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21987. No universal fitness.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21988. Fitness Function
> 
> Если использовать термин,
> 
> он всегда:
> 
> ```text
> Context-specific.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21989. Example
> 
> Architecture A:
> 
> ```text
> best latency
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21990. Architecture B:
> 
> ```text
> best energy efficiency
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21991. Different environments select differently.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21992. Поэтому лучше использовать:
> 
> ```text
> Requirement Satisfaction
> ```
> 
> чем универсальный fitness score.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21993. Variation Sources
> 
> ```text
> human design
> AI synthesis
> cross-domain transfer
> external technology
> forks
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21994. Artificial Technological Imagination generates variations.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21995. Synthesis Engine validates them.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21996. Programs test.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21997. Capability Capital retains successful results.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21998. Ecosystem Layer observes diffusion.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 21999. This completes:
> 
> ```text
> idea → ecosystem adoption
> ```
>

> 
> # 22000. Major milestone
> 
> К **22000** Innovation OS получает модель:
> 
> # Evolutionary Technological Ecosystem
> 
> где новые Capabilities:
> 
> ```text
> возникают
> проверяются
> распространяются
> комбинируются
> деградируют
> заменяются
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22001. Technology Lineage
> 
> Можно строить:
> 
> ```text
> Technology A
> ↓ derived/adapted
> Technology B
> ↓
> Technology C
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22002. Example
> 
> ```text
> fiber strain sensor
> ↓ adapted
> robot tactile strip
> ↓ integrated
> robot tactile skin
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22003. Lineage relations:
> 
> ```text
> DERIVED_FROM
> USES
> TRANSFORMS
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22004. Innovation Lineage preserves:
> 
> ```text
> origin
> adaptation
> evidence
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22005. This helps avoid:
> 
> ```text
> claiming isolated invention
> ```
> 
> where significant prior art exists.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22006. Lineage also supports:
> 
> ```text
> technology genealogy
> ```
> 
> for research.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22007. Architectural Lineage
> 
> Example:
> 
> ```text
> Cloud Architecture v1
> ↓
> Hybrid Edge v2
> ↓
> Local Autonomous v3
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22008. Each version influenced by:
> 
> ```text
> new requirements
> technology availability
> lessons
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22009. Lineage ≠ superiority sequence.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22010. Newer is not necessarily better for every Context.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22011. Forks
> 
> Technology may split:
> 
> ```text
> Version A
> ├─ branch B
> └─ branch C
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22012. Ecosystem can retain multiple branches.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22013. Example:
> 
> ```text
> high-performance
> low-power
> ```
> 
> variants.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22014. Fork Diversity
> 
> Useful if variants serve different niches.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22015. Niche
> 
> Can define as:
> 
> ```text
> Context where a Capability/Architecture
> has a distinctive requirement fit.
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22016. Example:
> 
> ```text
> cloud inference
> ```
> 
> niche:
> 
> ```text
> high compute / network available
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22017. Edge inference niche:
> 
> ```text
> low latency / local privacy
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22018. Neither universally replaces other.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22019. Niche Discovery
> 
> Cluster successful deployments by:
> 
> ```text
> Context
> Requirements
> Environment
> ```
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22020. Find where each technology performs well.
> 
> ---
> 
> # 22021. This is much better than:
> 
> ```text
> Technology X is best.

>

> 
> New technology may expand into:

> ```text
> new operational envelopes.

> ---
> 
> # 22023. Example local model becomes capable enough to handle tasks previously cloud-only.

> 
> # 22024. Ecosystem detects:
> 
> ```text
> niche expansion

> # 22025. Opportunity Engine reevaluates projects.

> ---
> 
> # 22026. Technology Substitution Wave

> ```text
> potential substitution paths

> # 22029. Instead:
>

> # 22030. Governance/owners decide migration.

> 
> # 22031. Recombination Engine
>

> 
> ```text
> Which capability pairs frequently complement each other?

> # 22032. Then seek:
> 
> ```text
> third capability

> +
> Vision

> # 22034. Add:

> ```text
> Tactile Sensing

> # 22035. New higher-order Capability:
> 
> ```text
> Delicate Manipulation
> ```

> ---
> 
> # 22036. This is evolutionary recombination.

> # 22038. This can accelerate innovation.

> # 22043. Ecosystem layer detects such phase transition.

> # 22045. Candidate platform indicators:
> 
> ```text
> cross-domain reuse

> # 22046. Platform Candidate ≠ Platform Decision.

> # 22047. Opportunity Engine may propose:

> # 22048. Commons Formation
> 
> Some shared assets behave like:
> 
> ```text
> knowledge commons

> 
> # 22049. Examples:
> 
> ```text
> open dataset
> open ontology
> open benchmark
> open-source package

> # 22050. Their value can grow through:

> ```text
> shared contribution

> 
> # 22051. Commons differs from commercial market.

> 
> # 22052. No assumption that every exchange requires payment.

> # 22053. Contribution Types
> 
> ```text
> code
> data
> documentation
> verification
> review
> infrastructure

> # 22054. Contribution ≠ Ownership automatically.

> 
> # 22055. Licensing/governance determines rights.

> # 22056. Contribution Provenance
>

> 
> ```text
> audit

> 
> # 22057. But avoid:
>

>

> not social ranking.

> ---

> 
> If needed for marketplace,

> # 22060. Example:
>

> 
> # 22061. Better than:
>

> # 22062. Keep verifiable history.
